rationale: Zakon and the Encyclopedia of Mathematics give the closure-interior definition of nowhere dense and the countable-union definition of meager. The local item also fixes residual and the second-category convention, so it is a bundled semantic restatement.
The Encyclopedia of Mathematics gives the same countable-union-of-closed and countable-intersection-of-open definitions, with the same ambient-real-line convention.

Both sources state Baire category for complete spaces and the dense-open-intersection form. The local statement specializes to the real line, adds the equivalent nonmeagerness clause, and makes the rational-endpoint construction canonical; its proof adapts the standard nested-set argument.

Zakon records that the rationals are meager and not G-delta and that a dense G-delta in a complete metric space is residual. The local item packages the complementary F-sigma/G-delta conclusions and supplies its own dependency-local proof.

MIT uses the epsilon-small countable interval-cover definition of nullity, while the UAF notes give the countable-cover formulation and the compact finite-subcover reduction. The local term content zero is a deliberately elementary finite-cover convention, so the package is a semantic restatement rather than an exact quotation of Jordan measure.

The UAF notes state the interval-cover length estimate used in the measure-zero argument and reduce compact interval covers to finite subcovers. The local proof changes the finite-overlap organization but proves the same covering estimate.

The UAF notes give the countable interval-cover argument showing that an interval of positive length is not null, using compactness to pass to a finite subcover. The local proof follows that argument with this library’s series indexing.

MIT Homework 2.1 states exactly that every countable subset of Euclidean space has measure zero. The local proof is the standard geometric-budget cover, adapted to zero-based indexing and the library’s countability convention.

MIT Homework 2.1 states exactly that a countable union of measure-zero sets has measure zero. The local proof expands the standard double-indexed epsilon allocation and explicitly records countable choice.
Finite covers are a special case of the countable interval covers in the MIT definition. The implication is a direct local verification from the two definitions; its proof is repository-local.

MIT Homework 2.4 states that compact-set measure can be computed with finite covers, semantically the nontrivial direction here. The local statement uses the library’s elementary null/content-zero vocabulary and adapts the open-cover argument.
The Chicago notes define the middle-thirds Cantor set by the same stagewise removal and intersection construction.

The sources identify the Cantor set with ternary expansions using only 0 and 2. The local theorem strengthens the presentation to a uniquely chosen digit sequence and an explicit bijection with binary sequences, and adapts the standard digit proof.

The sources give compactness, perfection, uncountability, nowhere density, total disconnectedness, and nullity of the middle-thirds set. The local item translates total disconnectedness into its available connected-subset vocabulary and proves the bundle locally.

The source describes the Smith-Volterra-Cantor construction by deleting successively smaller middle intervals and gives the stage lengths. The local definition encodes the same construction through explicit endpoint and length recursions.

The source gives a perfect nowhere-dense fat Cantor set of measure one half. The local statement avoids undeclared outer-measure vocabulary and replaces that value by the equivalent lower bound for every interval cover; the proof adapts the standard removal-length computation.

The Stanford source defines the Cantor function by converting ternary digits before the first 1 to binary digits and extending constantly across gaps. The local supremum formula is an equivalent, convention-clean construction.

The Stanford exercise states that the Cantor function is well defined, continuous, monotone, onto, and constant on complementary intervals. The local theorem selects the monotonicity, surjectivity, and gap-constancy clauses and proves them from its supremum definition.

The source distinguishes the ZF-provable separable complete case, including the real line, from the arbitrary complete-metric theorem equivalent to dependent choice. The local Remark narrows this to the canonical rational-endpoint proof and its dependency ledger.
The fat Cantor source supplies the standard nowhere-dense positive-measure counterexample. The false claim and its local refutation are a dependency-level restatement of that counterexample.
The sources together record that the rationals are dense and countable, hence null but not nowhere dense. The local false statement is refuted by exactly that standard witness.

MIT supplies the countable null-cover formulation and the UAF notes supply the compact finite-subcover argument. The local bounded-rational witness combines those standard facts to exhibit the failure of the converse without compactness.

Zakon states and proves the negation: the rationals are not a G-delta subset of the real line. The local displayed claim is the corresponding false statement, and its locally written refutation routes Zakon’s conclusion through the preceding Baire theorem.
The source states that the Cantor set is perfect and therefore uncountable. The local false claim isolates the familiar mistaken inference from countably many removed intervals.
The countable-set-null construction in MIT gives such an interval cover for any epsilon. The local item specializes it to a fixed enumeration of the rationals and computes the exact geometric budget.
The source gives the no-1 ternary membership criterion for the Cantor set. The local table works six values, including the alternating expansion of one quarter, so it is an altered worked example.

The source computes the total removed length of the Smith-Volterra-Cantor set as one half. The local example translates the result into a lower bound for interval-cover totals and derives it with the library’s finite-cover lemma.

Baire category implies that a complete metric space without isolated points is uncountable; the sources give the theorem and the rationals-as-meager example. The local proof is a fresh specialization to this dependency graph.

This is a positive bespoke-computation determination: the particular four-value table is not a named theorem or standard packaged example. Directly from the local digit definition, the middle third has binary value 0.1, one ninth has 0.01, one quarter has 0.010101..., and seven ninths has 0.11.

The Chicago source gives exactly the perfect and totally disconnected properties. The local example recasts the latter as every connected subset being a singleton and derives both clauses from preceding items.
The source explicitly presents the Smith-Volterra-Cantor set as nowhere dense with positive measure. The local counterexample delegates the two properties to its proved construction.
The sources give density and meagerness of the rationals and nullity of countable sets. The local counterexample combines these standard clauses; its proof is dependency-local.

MIT licenses countable nullity, and the UAF notes give the compact finite-subcover length argument for intervals. The local witness Q intersect [0,1] combines them to separate nullity from finite-cover content zero.

The Encyclopedia of Mathematics states that a meager subset of the real line can have full Lebesgue measure and that residual null sets exist. The local proof constructs such a decomposition explicitly from interval covers of the rationals.

This is a positive bespoke-witness determination: the item singles out one quarter rather than citing a named result. Its unique alternating 0,2 ternary sequence is not eventually constant, whereas every removed-gap endpoint has an eventually constant permitted expansion, so the witness is verified directly.
Zakon gives exactly that the rationals are not G-delta; complementation gives exactly that the irrationals are not F-sigma, while the same exercise records their residual G-delta form.
Zakon gives the same relative epsilon-delta definition on a subset. The local definition additionally packages the function-limit equivalence at limit points and the automatic isolated-point case.
Lebl presents the sequential criterion for continuity. The local statement keeps arbitrary subdomains and records the countable-choice cost of the converse, so it is a convention-aware adaptation.

The MIT notes list sums, products, quotients, composites, and polynomial continuity as the standard continuity algebra. The local theorem bundles absolute value, max, and min and expands epsilon-delta proofs in its dependency vocabulary.

The MIT notes state continuity of composite maps. The local statement has the same domain and pointwise hypotheses and contrasts them with punctured function limits; the proof is the standard epsilon-delta substitution.
The sources state that continuity is equivalent to open preimages, with the relative-domain trace convention. The local item adds the dual closed-set form and proves both directions.

Both sources state that the continuous image of a compact set is compact. The local proof is an altered, choice-conscious open-cover argument, with the empty image handled explicitly before the nonempty finite-subcover construction.
The Encyclopedia of Mathematics states that every real-valued continuous function on a compact space is bounded. The local corollary derives this immediately from compact image and Heine-Borel.

The source states that a continuous real-valued function on compact space attains its largest and smallest values. The local theorem makes nonemptiness explicit and proves attainment from compactness of the image.
Zakon states the intermediate value theorem for a continuous real function on an interval. The local proof adapts the standard bisection argument with a canonical left-half rule.
The source identifies the Darboux property with interval images. The local corollary derives order-convexity from IVT and adds the closed-bounded-image conclusion via compactness.

Conrad’s introduction states exactly that every continuous self-map of an arbitrary closed interval has a fixed point and proves it by applying IVT to f(x)-x. The local proof is that argument in the reversed sign convention.

Zakon proves that a monotone function with the Darboux property on an interval is continuous, including relative endpoint continuity. The local hypothesis that the image is order-convex is exactly the Darboux property for a monotone map.
Lebl gives the same epsilon-delta definition with one delta serving all pairs in the domain.

The sources give the metric versions of continuity, uniform continuity, Lipschitz conditions, and compactness on real subspaces. The local item is a direct dictionary across already defined notions, with convention details written out.

The sources state that a continuous function on a compact set is uniformly continuous. The local proof adapts the standard sequential contradiction and explicitly accounts for its countable selection.

The MIT problem states the unique extension of a uniformly continuous map from a dense subset into a complete target. The local corollary specializes to real subspaces and records that the extension remains uniformly continuous.
Cornell’s notes state exactly that the only alpha-Hölder functions for alpha greater than one are constant. The local proof expands the standard equal-partition estimate for rational exponents.

Rudin Theorem 4.20 states exactly the three clauses: on noncompact E there are an unbounded continuous function and a bounded continuous function with no maximum, and bounded noncompact E supports a non-uniformly-continuous continuous function. The local proof follows that theorem.
Lebl gives one over x on (0,1) as continuous but not uniformly continuous. The local false statement delegates to that explicit witness.
The MIT notes distinguish compact-image preservation from closed-image preservation. The local refutation uses the standard closed domain [1,infinity) under reciprocal, whose image is (0,1].
The source explains that EVT needs a closed bounded interval and that open intervals can lose attained extrema. The local witness is the identity on (0,1).
Heinonen states that distance to any set is 1-Lipschitz. The local example specializes to the integers and adds the exact range [0,1/2] and zero set.
Zakon gives exactly the rational indicator and proves that it is discontinuous at every real because rationals and irrationals meet every neighbourhood. The local proof is the same density argument.
The open text states exactly that x times the rational indicator is continuous at zero and nowhere else. The local proof expands both cases without sequences.
Lebl states exactly that one over x on (0,1) is not uniformly continuous. The local item uses an explicit zero-based pair sequence.
The source gives x squared on the real line as a standard continuous but not uniformly continuous example. The local item fixes explicit pairs compatible with zero-based indexing.

The university thesis proves that x to the alpha is alpha-Hölder, while the Wisconsin exercise uses power functions to separate Hölder orders. The local item combines these into the precise rational-exponent noninclusion statement.

The Rutgers examination solutions give exactly f(x)=g(x)=x on the real line as uniformly continuous factors whose product x squared is not uniformly continuous. This live source supersedes the inaccessible Johns Hopkins Spring 2019 solutions URL.
The source contrasts EVT on closed bounded intervals with open or unbounded domains. The local item packages the identity on (0,1) and on [0,infinity) as the two elementary witnesses.

The source gives IVT as the standard existence mechanism for roots of continuous equations. The local example specializes to x to the n on an explicitly bounded interval and checks both endpoint signs.

This is a positive bespoke-computation determination: the particular map x mapped to (x+2/x)/2 on [1,2] is a locally chosen worked example. Direct algebra shows its fixed points satisfy x squared equals 2, and the preceding fixed-point theorem supplies existence.
